query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration, low‐temperature post‐solidification annealing treatment can simultaneously improve both the room-temperature tensile strength and ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys by healing and strengthening the internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) featuring a fine lamellar fcc/B2 dual-phase microstructure with numerous internal boundaries that act as microcrack nucleation sites.
generation.intervention: Apply a short-duration annealing treatment at a low (subcritical) temperature that is high enough to promote limited interfacial diffusion for boundary healing but low enough to avoid lamellar coarsening.
generation.conditions: The treatment is conducted post-solidification under identical cooling and casting conditions, with room-temperature tensile testing. The annealing temperature and time must be carefully controlled to ensure that only interfacial healing occurs without altering the overall lamellar morphology.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced cohesion at the internal lamellar boundaries due to mild interfacial diffusion and healing.
generation.mechanism: The controlled annealing treatment promotes limited diffusion at the interfaces between the dual-phase lamellae, thereby healing weak spots and reducing the likelihood of microcrack initiation during loading. This reinforced interface enhances load transfer during deformation, concurrently boosting both tensile strength and ductility relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed alloys are expected to show statistically significant improvements in both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to as-cast specimens. Microscopy should reveal fewer and less severe microcracks initiating from the lamellar boundaries.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic alloy exhibits high strength but limited ductility due to brittle failure initiated at the numerous weak internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The improvement will only occur if the annealing temperature is below the threshold for lamellar coarsening and the duration is short enough to restrict changes only to interfacial bonding; excessive temperature or time could destabilize the fine lamellar structure.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature and duration required to achieve the desired interfacial healing without triggering lamellar coarsening remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of EHEA specimens: one set as-cast (baseline) and another subjected to the controlled low-temperature, short-duration annealing treatment. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets, and perform detailed microscopic analyses (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess interfacial integrity and monitor microcrack initiation sites during deformation.
measurements: Microstructural observations of lamellar boundaries (presence and evolution of microcracks)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed specimens do not exhibit statistically improved tensile strength and ductility relative to the as-cast baseline, or if microscopic analysis shows no reduction (or an increase) in microcrack nucleation at the inter-lamellar boundaries, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys, notably as shown in PMC4145285, established that the fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure can yield high strength, but the numerous internal (inter-lamellar) boundaries remain the loci for microcrack initiation, leading to brittle tensile behavior at room temperature. Subsequent attempts focused on modifying lamellar spacing, phase volume fractions, and hierarchical structuring via various processing and microstructural-design strategies. Although these efforts improved strength, they invariably compromised ductility because the weak, cracking‐prone interfaces were not adequately reinforced.
decision.unsolved: The critical unsolved issue is how to concurrently improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility by specifically strengthening the internal boundaries of the dual-phase lamellar colonies—without altering the overall lamellar morphology or introducing extra phases. Conventional processing enhances one property at the expense of the other, leaving microcracking at the interfaces unmitigated.
decision.lever: Apply a short-duration, low‐temperature post‐solidification annealing treatment (at a subcritical temperature that avoids lamella coarsening) designed to promote mild interfacial diffusion and healing at the lamellar colony boundaries.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of previous efforts by retaining the lamellar structure while directly targeting the weakness at the internal boundaries. By enhancing interfacial cohesion through controlled annealing, the treatment is hypothesized to reduce microcrack nucleation during tensile deformation, thereby simultaneously improving both strength and ductility relative to the unmodified baseline. Prior evidence (e.g., PMC4145285) underscores the importance of microstructural refinement in these alloys, and similar controlled thermal treatments have improved interfacial bonding in related systems. An experiment comparing room-temperature tensile tests of as-solidified versus low-temperature annealed specimens, with failure initiation monitored at the lamellar interfaces, would falsify the hypothesis if the annealed alloys fail to show reduced microcracking and improved ductility under identical strength levels.
